planting.note: Plant dormant bulbs in fall at the base of oaks or under open shrub canopy on a raised bed or slope; keep bone-dry through summer dormancy.

directions: A nodding, waxy-golden lantern flower held on wiry stems, this species is one of the few Calochortus that genuinely tolerates woodland shade, making it a rare shade-compatible mariposa-lily option for native and rock gardens under oaks. Plant in gritty, fast-draining soil where summer irrigation naturally stays away from the bulb, giving it winter and spring moisture but bone-dry summer dormancy. Treat exactly like the already-present white fairy lantern, except this species can take more shade.

planting.note: Plant dormant bulbs in fall in a raised, sharply drained scree or under an eave so winter rain and snowmelt doesn't pool; winter wetness, not cold, is the limiting cultivation factor.

directions: Small, understated flowers with greenish-white petals marked by a purple crescent and densely hairy inner surfaces carpet open conifer and oak understory in the wild, giving this a genuinely cold-hardy, shade-tolerant bulb for rock gardens in colder climates where most Calochortus fail. The limiting factor in cultivation is winter wetness, not cold, so grow in a raised, sharply drained scree or under an overhang. Best suited to growers in the Pacific Northwest interior and Rocky Mountain states who can mimic its native open-forest, well-drained gravel habitat.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 2 inches deep in fall before November into well-drained soil at a seasonally damp meadow or swale edge; cut off water abruptly after bloom to trigger proper summer dormancy.

directions: Loose clusters of one to five bell-shaped white-to-pink flowers with purple basal spotting naturally grow in moist meadows, making this one of the more forgiving Calochortus for gardeners who can't guarantee bone-dry summers. Give it more moisture during the growing season than typical dry-chaparral Calochortus — a seasonally damp meadow simulation such as a swale edge or vernal-pool margin suits it better than a pure rock garden. Rot remains the main failure mode if summer water continues past the normal dormancy trigger.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall under deciduous oaks in dappled light with well-drained, leaf-litter-covered duff; still needs a true dry summer, so avoid combining with summer-irrigated shade perennials.

directions: Bright, upright yellow starry flowers with densely bearded, clawed petals and a red-brown basal spot make this one of the most shade-flexible Calochortus, tolerating full sun, partial shade, or deep shade. Because it tolerates deep shade, it's a good candidate for underplanting beneath deciduous oaks where most Calochortus would fail from too much shade. It still needs a true dry summer, so keep it apart from summer-irrigated shade companions.

planting.note: Plant the bulb base at three times bulb height depth in decomposed granite or rocky slope soil; leave undisturbed once established rather than dividing, since it's intolerant of being moved.

directions: Among the most vividly colored Calochortus, this species carries vivid orange to scarlet cup flowers with a dark basal spot, extremely drought-tolerant and a showpiece for desert or xeric native gardens where almost nothing else in the genus will thrive on so little water. It is notably intolerant of being moved or divided once settled, so site it permanently in a true desert-garden setting. Avoid any supplemental summer water, even for neighboring plants, since root-zone moisture during dormancy is the main cause of failure.
sources: Theodore Payne Foundation Native Plant Database

planting.note: Plant bulbs about 4 inches deep in fertile, sharply-drained loam in full sun; avoid any site with summer irrigation runoff.

directions: A high-elevation Rocky Mountain native with purple-and-white cupped flowers, this is the most cold-hardy, continental-climate-adapted mariposa lily, giving Rocky Mountain and Great Plains gardeners a true native option for xeric meadow and rock-garden plantings. This species handles real winter cold far better than the California coastal species, making it the best choice for continental-climate rock gardens and high-altitude xeriscapes. Leaves die back just before flowering each year thereafter, so pair with companions that fill the visual gap.

planting.note: Plant the bulb base at three times bulb height depth in fall on a rocky, open slope with excellent drainage; never irrigate in summer once established.

directions: Large bright-yellow flowers with a cup packed with distinctive club-tipped hairs make this a strong chaparral-adjacent bulb, and its tolerance of partial shade gives it placement flexibility between open chaparral and oak-woodland edges that stricter full-sun Calochortus can't handle. It's taller and more floriferous than many Calochortus, so give it some support from neighboring shrubs in windy sites rather than staking. Rocky, open slopes with excellent drainage are essential regardless of sun exposure.

planting.note: Plant the bulb base at three times bulb height depth in fall into genuinely rocky or heavy dry soil mimicking chaparral slope drainage; plant several bulbs since not all will bloom every year.

directions: Branching stems bearing oval to wedge-shaped petals ranging from cream through deep yellow to reddish-purple give this chaparral species striking color variability. Don't expect annual blooming — this species' habit of skipping flowering years after a bloom is normal, not a cultivation failure, so plant several bulbs to ensure some are flowering most seasons. It needs genuinely rocky or heavy dry soil rather than light sandy mixes, mimicking chaparral slope drainage rather than desert-flat conditions.
